title: Collection Systems and Wet-Weather Response
audience: Practising wastewater operators and supervisors seeking focused applied development.
prerequisites: Basic operator terminology, metric calculations and access to the source readings. Use a calculator; all supplied facility data are fictional.
introduction: Analyse a fictional lift station and sewer catchment during rainfall. Calculate storage time, distinguish inflow from infiltration evidence, and prepare an incident record with honest volume uncertainty.
delivery: Self-paced online pilot with four practical modules, source reading, asynchronous instructor review of written work, a server-graded final assessment and evaluation. Breaks are excluded. Planned duration requires a timed pilot; no approved CEUs are awarded.

modules.title: Wet-weather patterns and catchment evidence
objectives: Calculate peak and daily flow changes.
Distinguish plausible inflow/infiltration patterns from proof.
modules.lesson:
### A hydrograph suggests where to investigate
Collection-system flow can include sanitary wastewater, infiltration through defects and inflow through direct connections. A rapid response to rainfall can suggest direct inflow; a sustained delayed response can suggest infiltration or storage effects. These are investigation clues, not definitive source identifications. Catchment travel time, pumping and rainfall distribution can alter the pattern.

Compare a wet period with a representative dry baseline. Peak ratio is wet peak divided by dry peak, while excess daily volume is wet daily volume minus the selected dry baseline. These quantities answer different questions. A brief peak may challenge capacity without dominating daily volume.

A baseline should account for weekday/weekend demand, seasonal groundwater, known industrial discharges and meter quality. Subtracting a convenient low-flow day can overstate rainfall-related volume. Preserve the rationale and test sensitivity to plausible baselines.

Use the pattern to target records review, authorized inspection and monitoring. The course does not direct entry into manholes, confined spaces or traffic zones. Physical investigation requires the appropriate trained crew and site procedures.
modules.evidence:
**C1 — South Branch catchment**
Dry comparable daily volume 2,400 m³; dry peak 180 m³/hour. Rain-day volume 3,600 m³; peak 420 m³/hour beginning 20 minutes after intense rain. Flow remains above baseline for 18 hours. A second plausible dry baseline is 2,600 m³/day. Rain gauge is 5 km from the catchment.

C2: No property connection testing or defect inspection has been completed. Flow meter quality checks are current but rainfall spatial coverage is uncertain.
modules.assignment: Calculate peak ratio and excess volume for both baselines. Prepare a 350–500-word investigation brief separating rapid and sustained response hypotheses. Rank three evidence requests, explain baseline and rainfall limitations, and assign field work to authorized personnel rather than prescribing unsafe access.
rubric: Does not identify a source from timing alone.
Uses baseline sensitivity and targeted evidence requests.
modules.facilitatorGuide: 420/180=2.333. Excess volumes are 1,200 and 1,000 m³; the alternative baseline changes the estimate by 200 m³. Both rapid and sustained components may be present, but pumping/storage and rainfall coverage remain alternatives. Strong requests include time-aligned rain/flow, pump operations and authorized asset/connection investigations. No definitive illegal-connection claim is supported.

modules.title: Wet-well storage and time to a trigger
objectives: Calculate net accumulation and conditional time remaining.
Explain why rated pump capacity may differ from actual delivery.
modules.lesson:
### Time remaining depends on the net rate
When inflow exceeds delivered outflow, stored volume increases at the difference. Conditional time to a stated level is available volume divided by net accumulation. If 90 m³ remains and inflow exceeds outflow by 30 m³/hour, the simple estimate is 3 hours. If inflow changes, the estimate changes; it is not a guaranteed response window.

Use actual delivered pumping at the current condition when supported. A pump's nameplate rating or command does not establish its current flow. Head, equipment condition, blockage and parallel operation can change delivery. Two nominal capacities do not necessarily add to the actual combined duty point.

If level data are used to infer storage, the level-to-volume relation must match the wet-well geometry. A constant area assumption works only over the stated range. Dead volume below the operating level is not available buffer above it.

Use the calculation to support escalation and resource planning under the authorized response procedure. Do not deliberately operate to the last calculated minute. Include uncertainty, trend updates and contingency ownership; do not propose unauthorized bypassing or equipment isolation.
modules.evidence:
**C3 — fictional lift station at 10:00**
Available volume to the supplied operational trigger 120 m³. Inflow 310 m³/hour; verified combined pump delivery 270 m³/hour. Nameplates suggest 320 m³/hour. At 10:30, cumulative stored volume has increased 25 m³; updated inflow 330 and delivery 280 m³/hour. The available-volume calculation is valid for this level range.

C4: Backup equipment availability is unconfirmed; no bypass authorization is supplied.
modules.assignment: Calculate the 10:00 conditional time and updated 10:30 time using the observed storage increase and new rates. Explain the error from using nameplate capacity. Draft a 300–450-word escalation note with assumptions, immediate evidence requests, trend update intervals and assigned contingency decisions.
rubric: Uses actual storage change rather than assuming the first rate stayed constant.
Treats times as conditional and preserves authority boundaries.
modules.facilitatorGuide: Initial net 40 m³/hour gives 3 hours. At 10:30 remaining 95 m³; net 50 gives 1.9 hours from 10:30, or nominal 12:24 if constant. Nameplate 320 would incorrectly imply no accumulation at the initial 310 inflow. Require prompt procedure-based escalation, verification of backup readiness and ongoing monitoring; no promise that 12:24 is safe or exact.

modules.title: Incident timelines and uncertain volumes
objectives: Estimate volume using stated interval assumptions.
Separate detection time from event onset.
modules.lesson:
### A volume estimate needs an evidence boundary
An incident may begin before it is detected. Record first evidence, detection, notification, observed conditions, actions and verified end separately. If onset is unknown, do not backfill it with the first alarm time and call it exact.

For a constant assumed rate, volume is rate multiplied by duration. For changing rates with discrete observations, an interval method such as trapezoidal integration can provide an estimate: average adjacent rates times the interval. State the interpolation assumption and any gaps. A calculated decimal does not make sparse observations precise.

Bounds may be more honest than one number. If an unobserved 15-minute interval plausibly ranged 0–20 m³/hour, that interval contributes 0–5 m³ under the supplied bound. Add it as a range, not as a fabricated measurement. These bounds are training assumptions; real estimates require defensible field evidence and the applicable reporting process.

Preserve initial estimates and subsequent revisions with time, author and reason. Reporting an updated estimate should not erase what was known when the first notification was made. Apply Ontario and facility-specific reporting requirements through the responsible role; the US reference supplies technical context, not local legal thresholds.
modules.evidence:
**C5 — fictional release-rate observations**
11:00 rate 20 m³/hour;11:15 rate 40;11:30 rate 0 with verified cessation at 11:30. For the observed interval, the case permits linear interpolation. Prior interval 10:45–11:00 is unobserved; supplied credible rate bound 0–20 m³/hour. Onset before 10:45 is excluded by a verified dry inspection at 10:45.

C6: First alarm 11:05; supervisor notified 11:10. An initial report says “Started 11:05, total 10 m³ exactly.”
modules.assignment: Calculate the observed interval volume and total range including the prior gap. Produce a timeline and a 400–550-word correction note to C6. Separate detection from onset, state interpolation/bound assumptions, preserve the original estimate and identify the reporting owner and missing evidence.
rubric: Does not use 11:05 as known onset.
Preserves estimates and discloses method uncertainty.
modules.facilitatorGuide: 11:00–11:15 mean 30×.25=7.5 m³; next mean 20×.25=5; observed 12.5. Prior interval adds 0–5, total 12.5–17.5. The alarm is detection evidence, not onset. Reject “exact” volume language and invented Ontario reporting thresholds. Ask what additional records could narrow the prior interval and who updates the formal report.

modules.title: Collection-system response and recovery plan
objectives: Prioritize capacity, evidence and communication tasks.
Define verified recovery and longer-term investigation.
modules.lesson:
### Recovery is an evidence-based milestone
A falling level can show improvement at a wet well while other parts of the catchment remain stressed. A pump running again does not prove its delivered flow, and a stopped release does not complete every reporting or follow-up duty. Define each recovery milestone and the evidence needed to mark it complete.

Structure the plan by immediate response, verification and longer-term investigation. Immediate work follows authorized incident procedures. Verification confirms delivered pumping, level trend, affected locations and cessation where relevant. Longer-term work examines rainfall response, defects, capacity and operational changes using the records preserved during the event.

Give each task an owner and a next decision point. Do not combine “requested,” “in progress” and “verified complete” into one checkbox. A clear register lets the next shift see where support is needed and prevents assumed closure.

The debrief should test the plan under a change in inflow or equipment availability. Recalculate the conditional storage time, revise priorities and state what remains uncertain. A good plan adapts without hiding its earlier assumptions.
modules.evidence:
**C7 — handover at 11:35**
Release cessation at 11:30 verified as inC5. Wet-well level falling at the last two readings; current verified outflow 340 m³/hour and inflow 300. Backup pump availability still unconfirmed. No downstream inspection completion record. The release-volume report still containsC6's original estimate.

C8: Manager asks to close all work orders because the level is falling.
modules.assignment: Prepare a 500–750-word handover with calculation appendix, immediate/recovery/investigation task register, owners and closure evidence. Correct the volume estimate, explain what C7 establishes, and respond to C8 without treating all tasks as equivalent. Discuss a scenario where inflow rises to 380 m³/hour, then complete the assessment and evaluation.
rubric: Separates cessation, hydraulic recovery, reporting and investigation.
Corrects volume and recalculates net accumulation under the changed inflow.
Uses owners and verification rather than blanket closure.
modules.facilitatorGuide: Current net draining 40 m³/hour supports local improvement. At 380 inflow with 340 outflow, accumulation resumes at 40 m³/hour; time to trigger cannot be calculated without current available volume. Cessation is verified, but report revision, downstream evidence and backup readiness remain open. Require a defensible incident record and procedure-based follow-up, not an invented legal determination.
